unit.sep: Observe, ask questions, collect and analyse data, infer and evaluate explanations.
unit.careers: Weather/climate science and human-health research: examine printed institutional evidence and investigate training separately.
unit.focus: Use evidence to explain the value of General Science and distinguish observation from inference.
unit.phenomenon: A school notice board has confident scientific claims, but some claims go beyond the observations.
unit.supportingPhenomena: Wet-window evidence, paper absorption data and seedling records with competing explanations.
unit.drivingQuestion: How can we turn observations into useful, defensible explanations? KICD: How is General Science useful in daily life?
unit.storylineThread: Everyday questions → observation/inference → data collection → competing causes → careers → communication → independent transfer.
unit.coreCompetencies:
Self-efficacy: as the learner designs and presents charts on career opportunities related to General Science and identifies a particular career path of own interest.
Digital literacy: as the learner uses digital media to research on the scientific processes, importance of General Science and careers related to General Science.
Citizenship: as the learner draws a chart on careers related to General Science and identifies with a particular career path for individual and national development.
unit.values:
Respect: as the learner appreciates others’ opinions when discussing the importance of General Science in day-to-day life.
Responsibility: as the learner uses digital devices appropriately to search for information on the career opportunities related to General Science.
unit.pcis: Socio-Economic and Environmental Issues: as the learner discusses with peers the importance of General Science to the environment and technology.
unit.content: Importance of General Science,; Careers in General Science; The principle of inference as used in science education

assessment.instructions: Lesson 7:4 minutes reading/procedure,28 minutes for sections 1–4 (16 for sections 1–2 and 12 for sections 3–4),4 minutes for a separate still-open-question reflection, and 4 minutes checking/collection; total 40. Work independently using GS17 only; basic calculator optional. Explain your reasoning, distinguish observations from inferences and label suggested uses/career activities as examples. No teaching cards.

sections.title: 1. What is General Science useful for?
sections.prompt: Explain General Science as a learning area. Use the new material-testing case to connect evidence to a possible technology decision, and give one different life/environment example. State one limitation of applying the test result.
sections.exemplar: General Science connects inquiry and knowledge about living things, matter and physical processes. Testing material properties can inform a proposed design choice, but water-rise data alone cannot show that a material is always best. A garden comparison can inform questions about plant conditions, but needs comparable conditions to isolate a cause. Accept another reasoned life/environment link.

sections.title: 2. Observation, analysis and inference
sections.prompt: Calculate both means. State one observation, an inference supported by the test and an alternative explanation for the difference. Evaluate the poster’s “always best” claim and propose one design change that would improve the comparison.
sections.exemplar: Means X14 mm and Y8 mm. Water-line readings and recorded conditions are observations; greater mean rise for X under the tested conditions is supported. Unequal sunlight may contribute to the difference; it is not ruled out. “Always best” exceeds both the property measured and the tested conditions. Test both materials under comparable light with fresh repeated strips, keeping other relevant conditions comparable. Other justified alternatives accepted. Scoring clarification: the computed mean comparison may be called descriptive data analysis rather than inference. Accept that distinction. A suitable tentative inference is that material properties or exposure conditions may contribute to the difference; this confounded design cannot isolate either cause. Do not require a confident causal explanation.

sections.title: 3. Career evidence
sections.prompt: Use both printed source summaries to identify two related career directions. For each give a possible science question or evidence type, label it as your proposed example, and say what the source actually supports. State one thing about training these summaries cannot establish.
sections.exemplar: Weather/climate science can use instrument records to investigate rainfall patterns; the source states observation/analysis/forecast roles but the question is a proposed example. Human-health research can investigate a properly governed health-study question; the source supports a human-health research role rather than a specified personal duty. The summaries do not establish an entry qualification, duration, salary or guaranteed employment.

sections.title: 4. Reasoned reflection
sections.prompt: Explain one way careful scientific reasoning could benefit your daily life. Identify one next learning action and explain why it would help. You may choose any relevant context; no particular career choice is required.
sections.exemplar: An appropriate answer links a concrete decision to checking evidence and limits, then proposes an attainable action such as practising observation/inference classification or verifying a training question with an official source. Judge the reasoning and specificity, not the chosen preference or a claim to lasting attitude change.

rubric.criterion: Explain General Science and a defensible use
rubric.excellent: Defines the learning area, explains both required application links and clearly limits what the material test can establish.
rubric.proficient: Explains the learning area and both application links with a relevant limitation.
rubric.developing: Gives a relevant use but the learning-area explanation or evidence link is incomplete.
rubric.belowExpectations: Needs guided work to distinguish a science example from a supported explanation.

rubric.criterion: Analyse evidence and evaluate an inference
rubric.excellent: Both means are correct; distinguishes observation/inference, explains a competing cause and gives a specific fairer design with a clear limit.
rubric.proficient: Both means and distinction are correct; gives a relevant alternative, rejects the overclaim and improves the design.
rubric.developing: Some relevant reasoning but calculation, distinction or comparison design needs correction.
rubric.belowExpectations: Needs guided support to extract observations or separate them from a claimed cause.

rubric.excellent: Both directions have appropriate labelled examples, exact source-role support and a clear training-information limit.
rubric.proficient: Identifies both directions with sensible examples and distinguishes source support from unverified training.
rubric.developing: One sound direction or an incomplete distinction between source and proposed activity.
rubric.belowExpectations: Needs guided reading to connect either source role to a career direction.

rubric.excellent: Links a concrete daily benefit to careful reasoning and an attainable action with a clear explanation of its value.
rubric.proficient: Gives a relevant benefit and next action with a reason.
rubric.developing: Benefit/action is relevant but the reasoning is vague or incomplete.
rubric.belowExpectations: Needs prompts to identify a specific benefit and learning action.
